take: Seamus is the rare brand where the manufacturing story and the product story are the same story. Akbar and Megan Chisti cut and sew in Beaverton rather than placing an order offshore, which is why the range can carry registered Irish tartans and licensed Pendleton wool at all — those are relationships and mill minimums, not prints.
The Glen Affric Tartan Driver at $130 makes the case on its own: a pattern dated to roughly the sixteenth century, fleece-lined, stretched over a titanium head. Nothing else in the bag does that.

This is for the walker who notices materials, and for anyone who wants one object in the bag that did not come out of the same factory as everyone else’s. A $36 ball marker is the cheapest way to find out whether you care; the covers run to $170.
story_extra: Seamus turns the headcover into the most personal object in the bag, in registered Irish tartans and licensed Pendleton wool, and the company started with one that was falling apart. Akbar Chisti’s father had given him a wool cover from a famous links club, Royal Troon by the company’s own telling, and it had worn through. His wife Megan was a womenswear designer at Pendleton Woolen Mills, so in 2011 she remade it from fabric remnants, sewed a few more for his golf group, and then the two of them were running a company out of their garage. It is named after their Irish Terrier, Seamus O’Reily, and you pronounce it SHAY-mus.

The first wholesale order came from Bandon Dunes, where Akbar had caddied in college. Fifteen years later the operation still cuts and sews everything in Beaverton, Oregon, in wool, leather, canvas and seersucker, with fabric from Pendleton and from UK mills including parliament-protected Harris Tweed. It wholesales to roughly 700 shops worldwide and the Chistis still own all of it.

Two things make Seamus more than a nice accessories company. The first is the 2016 Ryder Cup, when Matt Kuchar commissioned personalized American flag covers for the entire U.S. team: thirteen hand-cut stripes, fifty embroidered stars, each one sewn in Oregon. The second is the blacksmith. The Hand Forged line of markers, pitch tools and money clips is hammered rather than cast, by a smith in Portland who now does about ninety per cent of his business with Seamus. The USGA lets them set up and hammer markers on-site at U.S. Open merchandise pavilions, where the brand has sold every year since Chambers Bay in 2015.

The catalogue has three parts. Driver and fairway covers are the engine of the company, at $120 to $170. The putter shelf is where the fabric library shows off, in registered Irish tartans, Hawaiian barkcloth and licensed Pendleton patterns. The forged bench runs $36 to $76, and hand-stamped personalization on it is free.
